# The Heat Is Unequal: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

Summer in the city has always been hotter than summer in the countryside, but climate change has transformed a familiar discomfort into a genuine public health crisis. Urban heat islands—the phenomenon whereby cities run several degrees warmer than their surrounding regions—now kill more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. The question of how cities can make heat bearable is therefore not merely a matter of comfort. It is a question of survival, and, crucially, of whose survival. The tools available to cities are well understood: trees, street design, housing standards, and public transit. What is less understood is that these tools involve real tradeoffs, and that the burdens of those tradeoffs have historically fallen on the residents least able to bear them.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

Trees are the most intuitively appealing solution to urban heat, and for good reason. A mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath its canopy by as much as 15 degrees Fahrenheit through a combination of shade and evapotranspiration, the process by which leaves release water vapor.
